catalog_quote: The phrase stress group is the basic unit to which stress is assigned. All types of stress have the same phonetic cues. The primary cues for stress are change in pitch and the height of the resulting peak of pitch prominence: stressed high tones become falling tones which fall from a higher than usual pitch level and stressed low tones become rising tones which rise to a higher than usual level. ... Despite the fact that stressed syllables are more prominent than others, reduction of unstressed syllables is minimal, and Nigerian Pidgin can safely be said to be a syllable-timed language. ... sweep_summary: Two target items, both by Faraclas on Rivers Pidgin English (= Nigerian Pidgin nige1257). (1) Faraclas 1984, SLS 14(2):67-76 — already on file from the 9/16 pass (Illinois OCA djvu text of the volume), read in full: word-level 'stress' of English-derived words is a lexical H on the English-stressed syllable, realized as a stress-like contour only at the end of a pitch phrase / stress-accent group; substrate words are tonal; conclusion = mixed tone / pitch-accent / stress system with accentuation at the phrase level. Confirms the catalog's PHRASAL coding. (2) Faraclas 1985, 'Rivers Pidgin (Creole) English...', Studies in African Linguistics Supplement 9 (ACAL 15 précis, ed. Schuh) — fetched sources this sweep as the open full-issue PDF from journals.flvc.org (DOI 10.32473/sal.v16iSupp; saved as /.txt): a three-page précis of the SLS paper at pp. 111-113 (Glottolog's '67-76' is the SLS article's pagination, wrong for the supplement); same analysis ('phrase-level system of accentuation which is clearly stress-related'), confirms. Neither supersedes the catalog's deciding source, Faraclas 1996 (Routledge grammar), which is the same author's fuller later statement. Two on-disk extras read for completeness: Faraclas 2013 APiCS survey (confirms phrase stress + lexical tone; states the unmarked-word default H on the penult) and Oyelere 2021 thesis (instrumental; rejects word stress, argues lexical pitch-accent + tone, puts Faraclas' stress at the postlexical level — refines, does not contradict). Nothing left to acquire; priority none across the board. all look-ups were done with web lookups/curl against Glottolog and the SAL OJS site.

new_statements.quote: When RPE words are considered in isolation, it becomes apparent that the great majority (perhaps 85% - 90T [scanned; = 90%]) of words brought into the language from languages with stress-dominant pitch patterns (i.e. Portuguese, English, Spanish, etc.) bear a high (or, if word-final, falling) pitch over the syllable which bears stress in the source language and carry low pitch over the other syllables. [...] When not in isolation, the above outlined stress-like pitch patterns over Group A words occur only at the end of what will be called pitch phrases in this work. [...] At the surface, one is tempted to apply a stress analysis but the actual system is in many ways a reinterpretation of stress in terms of tone and pitch-accent.

new_statements.reading: Faraclas' first-hand 1984 analysis of the Rivers (Port Harcourt) dialect: English-derived words keep a lexical high pitch on the syllable that is stressed in English, but this shows up as a stress-like HL contour only when the word ends a pitch phrase (stress-accent group); elsewhere the H spreads rightward, and substrate-derived words are fully tonal and immune to phrase accentuation. The domain of accentuation is the phrase, the within-word peak is lexically specified (tone), and F0 is the only cue. This is exactly the phrase-stress-over-lexical-tone system that the catalog's deciding source (Faraclas 1996, the Routledge grammar) states in full, so the catalog's PHRASAL coding stands. The 1985 SAL Supplement 9 précis (fetched sources and read this sweep, pp. 111-113, not 67-76 as Glottolog lists) is a three-page summary of the same paper and adds only the yam/market phrasal-stress minimal pair.

Bearing as reported stands: Faraclas 1984 places the stress-like HL prominence at the right edge of the pitch phrase ("stress-accent group or phrase"), keeps the within-word H position as lexically specified (underspecified tone), notes F0 is the only cue, and exempts substrate (Class D) words - i.e. phrase-level accentuation over lexical tone, which is the catalog's PHRASAL coding. audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation, domain quote and exception quote are all verbatim in the held archive.org text of Faraclas 1996 at the cited sections and pages (3.3.2.2-3.3.2.4-6, pp. 260-263). (2) The classification rests on the standard Routledge reference grammar by the language's principal describer; the grammar's own pointer for stress/tone detail (Faraclas 1984, SLS 14(2)) was fetched sources from the University of Illinois open digitization and gives the same analysis in more detail (lexical, often underspecified tone on words; phrase-final H->fall / L->rise glide = phrase accent; explicit statement that a word-stress analysis fails in connected speech). Faraclas 2013 (APiCS, fetched sources) restates it. (3) The one newer dedicated prosody study, Oyelere 2021 (instrumental PhD, fetched sources from HAL), finds no convergence of duration and pitch on any syllable and concludes Naija is not a stress language

sources.citation: Faraclas, Nicholas. 2013. Nigerian Pidgin. In Michaelis, Maurer, Haspelmath & Huber (eds.), The survey of pidgin and creole languages, vol. 1. Oxford: OUP; APiCS Online survey chapter 17. [NOT in the target item list; on file from the 2026-09-16 pass and read in this sweep]
sources.quote: 'just as in other Nigerian languages, a phrase stress system also operates in Nigerian Pidgin, which converts the pitch over the final syllable in the phrase to which tone is underlyingly assigned from high to falling (high-low) or from low to rising (low-high). There is a class of lexical items, mostly from substrate languages, which are exempt from phrase stress'; 'polysyllabic words unmarked for tone carry a single lexical high tone over their penultimate syllable' (orthographic convention).
sources.locator: APiCS Online survey 17, section on phonology (suprasegmentals), example (2) 'Interaction of tone and phrase stress'
sources.note: Same author as the catalog source, later and condensed: lexical tone (H/L/!H/toneless) plus a phrase-stress system realized on the final tone-bearing syllable of the phrase as a contour; substrate words exempt. Adds an explicit default for word-level lexical tone placement (single H on the penult of unmarked polysyllables) which the catalog's phrasal record could cite as the within-word landing site, but Faraclas still codes it as tone, not stress.

sources.note: Instrumental corpus study (NaijaSynCor, ~3000 tokens, carrier sentences). Finds stable word-level pitch patterns (monosyllables /F/; bisyllables /HL/, /LF/, /LH/; trisyllables /HLL/, /LHL/, /LLF/, /HLF/, /HHF/), a single melodic peak per content word ('hat' pattern), and 'accentual sandhi' (final L/F of verbs, attributive adjectives, adverbs suspended before a complement). Rejects a word-stress analysis because duration does not co-vary with the high pitch; classifies the lexical system as pitch accent + tone (functors tonal). sources.citation: Faraclas, Nicholas. 1985. Rivers Pidgin (Creole) English: tone, stress, or pitch-accent language? In Russell G. Schuh (ed.), Précis from the 15th Conference on African Linguistics (UCLA, 1984), Studies in African Linguistics Supplement 9, pp. 111-113. (Glottolog ref 59395 gives 'Suppl. 9, 67-76' — the page range is wrong: 67-76 is the SLS 14(2) article; the précis is at pp. 111-113 of the supplement, checked in the issue TOC and body.)
sources.quote: The argument for a stress analysis of pitch phenomena in RPE is supported by the existence of a phrase-level system of accentuation which is clearly stress-related, the limited scope and primarily grammatical nature of almost all critical pitch distinctions in the language, and the clear correlation of stress placement over English words to the assignment of high pitch over most RPE words derived from English. An apostrophe precedes a syllable which receives phrasal stress-accent: /jam/ ['ja:m] 'yam' [a si maket 'ja:m] 'I found the market yams' /maket/ ['maket] 'market' [a si jam 'maket] 'I found the yam market' [p. 111]
sources.locator: pp. 111-112, secs. 1.1 'Arguments for a stress analysis' and 2 'RPE: A mixed system'
sources.note: Three-page conference précis of the SLS paper (same author, same data, same conclusion): accentuation is phrase-level ('phrasal stress-accent' on the final word of an accent group), the placement of the lexical high pitch inside English-derived words mirrors English stress, substrate-derived words are tonal and exempt from phrase-level stress-accent, F0 is the only reliable phonetic cue; the system is declared mixed (tone + pitch-accent + stress). Adds nothing beyond the 1984 article except the yam/market phrasal-stress minimal pair. Not a separate description; Faraclas himself cites the work…
